J. Quant. Anal. Sports 2026; aop
Research Article
Pavanthi Sudasinghe, Gary Parker, Hashan Peiris and Tim B. Swartz*
Analysis of pressing in soccer
https://doi.org/10.1515/jqas-2026-0001
Received January 2, 2026; accepted July 17, 2026; 
published online August 17, 2026
Abstract: This paper considers the tactic of pressing in soc-
cer. The investigation deﬁnes the conditions that constitute 
a traditional press, which then permits the identiﬁcation 
of pressing situations using tracking data.

The data con-
sist of matches from the 2019 season of the Chinese Super 
League. Descriptive analyses suggest that traditional press-
ing is associated with more turnovers when the pressed 
player is given less time on the ball and as the intensity of the 
press increases (i.e. more pressers). It is also observed that 
counter-pressing is associated with better outcomes than 
a traditional press. Statistical modeling provides further 
insights with respect to pressing.

For example, it is observed 
that pressing is associated with better outcomes when it is 
initiated deep and central in the opponent’s end of the ﬁeld.
Keywords: Bayesian analyses; Markov model; spatio-
temporal data; soccer tactics; transition matrices
1 Introduction
Pressing is a tactic that is widely used in soccer. When a 
team has possession of the ball in their defensive end, the 
opponent can choose to “press” with the intention of gaining 
possession.

We refer to this as traditional pressing. Although 
there are many versions of traditional pressing, the pressing 
team dedicates players to apply pressure. They do this by 
taking away time and space of the team in possession, and 
attempting to force a turnover.

There are various triggers that initiate a press.

For 
example, a press may depend on the location of the ball, 
the player in possession, the score of the match, the time 
of the match, whether the pressing team has recently lost 
possession, signals from the manager, etc.
There are also various ways that presses can be exe-
cuted. For example, the player in possession may be pres-
sured by multiple players, teammates in the vicinity of the 
player in possession may be tightly covered, passing lanes 
may be taken away by the pressing team, risky passes by 
the pressed team may be encouraged by the pressing team, 
etc.

Since pressing requires commitment and energy by the 
pressing team, pressing is a tiring tactic, which cannot be 
used during the entire match. Consequently, teams must 
judiciously decide when and how to press.
Given that pressing is such an integral part of soccer, it 
may be surprising that the topic of traditional pressing has 
not received more attention in the academic literature. One 
reason for this is that the complexities of pressing have been 
an impediment to both data collection and statistical anal-
yses.

On the other hand, various authors have considered 
“pressure” in various contexts. For example, Andrienko 
et al. (2017) develop visualizations and generate statistics 
for pressure situations applied by the defending team in 
their defensive end of the ﬁeld. However, these pressure 
situations in one’s own end of the ﬁeld are fundamentally 
different from traditional pressing in the attacking zone. 
The objectives and the implementation of applying pres-
sure by the defending team differs from traditional pressing 
which is executed by the attacking team.

In a related contri-
bution, Bojinov and Bornn (2016) produce spatial maps to 
inform team defensive weaknesses and strengths based on 
the concept of disruption.
Since the mechanics of pressing are complex, related 
work on the more general topic of transitions (i.e. change of 
possession) is more common. Some notable studies include 
Hughes and Lovell (2019) and Jamil (2019) who showed that 
winning possession in the offensive zone increases scoring 
compared to winning possession in other zones.

There is 
also evidence that scoring outcomes are improved following 
a transition if there is a rapid progression towards the goal 
(Maneiro et al. 2019).

2 — P. Sudasinghe et al.: Pressing in soccer
There are several papers that have investigated tradi-
tional pressing. For example, a recent preprint by Bekkers 
(2025) measures pressing intensity using player move-
ment and positional data. Brîndescu et al. (2021) analyze 
advanced pressing in the Premier League by looking at 
concepts such as line of engagement, pressing intensity, 
and defensive depth.

In their research, advanced press-
ing is examined in higher areas of the pitch, particularly 
the ﬁnal third, and teams are categorized into defensive 
blocks (high, medium, and low). Their approach depends 
on descriptive analysis and aggregate statistics (e.g., press-
ing success rates and positional summaries). Research con-
ducted by Forcher et al. (2022) examines pressure exerted 
throughout the pitch through spatial and temporal charac-
teristics derived from tracking data.

Their analysis focuses 
on deliberate attacks (a minimum of 5 s and three passes). It 
doesn’t include shorter and more dynamic situations. More-
over, success is only based on ball recovery. Other potential 
outcomes, like forcing the ball out of play, are not taken into 
account.
Our investigation of pressing is facilitated through 
tracking data. With tracking data, we know the location of 
the ball and all 22 players on the pitch measured at high 
frequency.

With tracking data and a workable deﬁnition 
of a press, we are able to isolate instances of pressing and 
form a relevant dataset. With the wealth of information 
contained in tracking data, there have been many recent 
novel investigations in soccer concerning player evaluation 
and tactics. For example, Anzer and Bauer (2021) develop 
expected goals (xG) models that reduce the luck component 
from match results.

Guan et al. (2023) consider the tactic of 
playing defensively when protecting a lead. In these inves-
tigations, it is the spatio-temporal knowledge of off-the-ball 
activities that provides additional insight that is unavailable 
with summary statistics contained in box score data. Statisti-
cal methods and analyses across major sports are discussed 
in the book by Albert et al. (2017).
In our development, we deﬁne a traditional press.

Although the deﬁnition may be modiﬁed to suit particu-
lar investigations, our deﬁnition is sufficiently broad to 
include many of the key elements associated with a variety 
of presses. In this paper, we attempt to better understand 
features and outcomes associated with pressing. Our study 
introduces several key extensions to the existing literature. 
We consider multiple outcomes of pressing success, includ-
ing not only turnovers but also situations where the ball 
is forced out of play.

We also consider sequence of passes 
following a pressing action until a ﬁnal outcome is reached. 
We also consider the counter-press which is a type 
of press where a team attempts to regain possession
immediately after losing possession in the offensive zone. 
The counter-press has become increasingly more common 
in recent years. It was popularized in the German Bun-
desliga by managers such as Ralf Rangnick (Leipzig) and 
Jürgen Klopp (Dortmund), and hence, counter-pressing is 
sometimes known by the term gegenpressing .

Gegenpress-
ing is less structured and may be thought of as chaotic since 
the primary objective is to recover the ball without regard 
to positioning. Consequently, counter-pressing sometimes 
appears as a scramble, and is studied separately from the 
traditional press.
In addition to the presentation of novel descriptive 
statistics associated with pressing, we develop statistical 
models. Since there are many outcomes associated with 
the execution of a press, we simplify the potential out-
comes by introducing a Markov assumption. The Markov 
assumption asserts that the immediate consequence from 
a press depends only on the state of the match immediately 
prior to the current time.

In Section 2, we describe the preliminaries needed for 
the analysis of pressing. The tracking data are ﬁrst intro-
duced. Then, we provide a deﬁnition of traditional pressing. 
Using tracking data, this allows us to construct a spread-
sheet where rows correspond to pressing situations. Var-
ious exploratory analyses are then carried out concern-
ing presses. In Section 3, statistical models are introduced 
that relate pressing outcomes to various pressing features.

Assumptions are made which lead to more parsimonious 
models that retain the essence of soccer. We consider both a 
traditional Markov transition model and a Bayesian model. 
In Section 4, we conclude with a short discussion.
2 Preliminaries
2.1 Data
For this investigation, we have a big data context where both 
event data and player tracking data are available for 233 reg-
ular season matches with seven matches missing from the 
2019 season of the Chinese Super League (CSL).

The schedule 
is balanced where each of the 16 teams plays every opponent 
twice, once at home and once on the road. In Table 1, we list 
the 16 teams and provide coded abbreviations used for each 
team.
Event data and tracking data are collected indepen-
dently where event data consist of match occurrences such 
as tackles and passes, and these are recorded along with 
auxiliary information whenever an “event” takes place.

The 
events are manually recorded by technicians who view 
ﬁlm. Both event data and tracking data have timestamps so

There are various ways in which tracking data are collected. 
One approach involves the use of RFID technology where 
each player and the ball have tags that allow for the accurate 
tracking of objects. In the CSL dataset, tracking data are 
obtained from video and the use of optical recognition soft-
ware. The tracking data consists of roughly one million rows 
per match measured on seven variables where the data are 
recorded every 1/10th of a second.

Each row corresponds 
to a particular player at a given instant in time. Although 
the conclusions gained via our analyses are speciﬁc to the 
CSL, we suggest that the methods are applicable to any 
soccer league which collects tracking data. The CSL is a 
strong league with international players, and it is believed 
that it shares many characteristics with other professional 
leagues.
2.2 Definition of a traditional press
Since presses take various forms and there does not seem 
to be a widely accepted deﬁnition of a press, we provide a 
deﬁnition that is general and can be modiﬁed to suit speciﬁc 
investigations.

In this study, the team in its own defensive 
end is referred to as the defensive team. We are interested 
in situations where they have possession of the ball. Based 
on our soccer knowledge, we propose four conditions that 
constitute a traditional press:
1. We stipulate that a press requires a defensive player to 
gain possession of the ball in their defensive end of the
pitch deﬁned as the ﬁnal third (from the point of view 
of the offensive team). Although presses may occur at 
other locations, the ﬁnal third is our primary interest, 
where possession typically involves defenders (i.e.

the 
left-back, the right-back or center backs). We refer to 
the pressed player as the player who has possession of 
the ball on the “pressed” team. 
Operationally, with tracking data, it is straightfor-
ward to identify the ﬁnal third of the pitch since the 
(x, y) location coordinates are available for each player.
2. We stipulate that pressure is applied to the pressed 
player with the intention of forcing a turnover.

Operationally, this is characterized by at least one 
player on the “pressing” team moving towards the 
pressed player. Speciﬁcally, this notion requires a press-
ing player moving at a speed that allows him to reach 
the pressed player in t seconds. For velocity smooth-
ing, we have used the methods recommended by Wu 
and Swartz (2023) which has been demonstrated to be 
reliable. Note that this requires the pressing player to 
be moving with pace if he is a considerable distance 
from the pressed player. Alternatively, if the pressing 
player is close to the pressed player, the pressing player 
does not need to be moving as quickly.

We consider 
t, the closeout time, as a tuning parameter, and we 
investigate the settings t < 1.5 s which we refer to as 
a hard-closeout, t ∈ (1.5, 2) seconds, which we refer to 
as a moderate-closeout, and t ∈ (2, 3) seconds which 
we refer to as a soft-closeout. 
The motivation for small t is that the pressed 
player does not have much time to make a decision 
before being tackled. With tracking data, we can cal-
culate player velocities and easily determine whether 
players are moving towards the pressed player with 
sufficient speed.

3. We stipulate that the pressing team is committed to the 
press in the sense that n players are involved in the 
press. Therefore, n is an intensity variable, and we will 
investigate the impact of the intensity on the outcome 
of the press. We refer to n = 2, 3 as a mild intensity 
press, and n ≥ 4 as a high intensity press. 
Operationally, this means that the complementary 
pressing players are attempting to eliminate the near-
est passing options of the pressed player. These pressing 
players are either (i) moving to cover nearby team-
mates of the pressed player or (ii) moving to take away 
passing lanes that are available to the pressed player. 
The passing lanes are those that provide an outlet pass 
to open players on the pressed team.
Movement to a

4 — P. Sudasinghe et al.: Pressing in soccer
passing lane is deﬁned as movement towards any point 
along the chord between the pressed player and a team-
mate of the pressed player.
4. The ﬁnal condition concerns the angle at which the 
pressing players approach the pressed player in posses-
sion. We are interested in presses that force the player 
in possession to rid themself of the ball. 
Operationally, this means that the pressed player 
does not have the option of dribbling unimpeded up 
the ﬁeld.

Pressure from behind is ineffective since the 
pressed player may simply dribble forward to open 
space. To implement this, at each frame we look at 
where the pressing player is relative to the ball and 
compare it to the forward direction of play on the 
pitch. We only keep cases where the pressing player is 
not approaching from behind the ball. In practice this 
means that the player has to be in an area in front of the 
ball (up to 90 ◦ to either side of the forward direction).

We note that the four conditions are assessed by advancing 
through the tracking data frame by frame. When the four 
conditions are satisﬁed, this constitutes a press and provides 
a row for our pressing spreadsheet. The columns of the 
spreadsheet (described later) consist of variables of interest 
related to the press (e.g., the score of the match, the time of 
the match, the outcome of the press, etc.).

We have developed efficient code which creates the 
pressing spreadsheet in roughly 20 h; this does not include 
the time required for model ﬁtting. The computations were 
carried out on a laptop with a 13th Gen Intel ® Core™ i5-
1335U processor (1.30 GHz) and 8 GB of RAM.
2.3 Descriptive statistics for the traditional 
press
We provide some exploratory investigations involving 
presses. To our knowledge, no such work has been previ-
ously carried out.

We are interested in the two parameters that were 
introduced in the deﬁnition of the traditional press. Accord-
ing to condition #2, we are interested in the closeout time 
t in seconds, the time until the presser reaches the pressed 
player. According to condition #3, we are also interested in 
the intensity of the press, measured by the number of offen-
sive players n that are involved in the press.

The choice of t 
and n is somewhat arbitrary. We experimented with differ-
ent choices, and these did not yield meaningful differences. 
We are interested in how these two parameters t and 
n relate to the outcome of the traditional press. Speciﬁcally, 
we investigate the proportion of time OB that the ball goes 
out of bounds and the proportion of time TO that there is a 
turnover. From the point of view of the pressing team, large 
values of OB and TO are indicative of pressing success.

In Table 2, we have recorded 7,596 traditional presses. 
We observe that traditional pressing is associated (i.e. both 
larger OB and larger TO) with harder closeouts (i.e. smaller 
t). This relationship is nearly monotonic in Table 2, and cor-
responds to our soccer intuition that it is more challenging 
for the pressed player when less time is available. Similarly, 
from Table 2, we observe that effective traditional press-
ing (larger OB and larger TO) is associated with increased 
intensity n of the press.

This relationship is monotonic and 
corresponds to our intuition that it is more challenging for 
the pressed player when more offensive players commit to 
pressing. Given that we have large sample sizes N , these 
results do not appear to be spurious.
Next, we investigate the variability of traditional press-
ing across teams and matches. In Figure 1, we provide box-
plots of the number of pressing occasions per game for each 
of the CSL teams in 2019.

We observe that teams press about 
15 times per match on average. It appears that Shanghai 
SIPG presses the most frequently with an average exceeding 
20 times per match. However, the variability across games 
is large. For example, most teams have matches where they 
press as little as ﬁve times. On the other hand, some teams 
may press as often as 40 times in a match.

Figure 1: Boxplots of the number of traditional presses per game executed by CSL teams.
We next investigate whether there are differences in 
pressing outcomes across the CSL teams. In Figure 2, we pro-
vide barplots of the turnover rates for each of the 16 teams. 
Here, we observe differences across teams. We observe that 
high-turnover teams create turnovers roughly 35 % of the 
time whereas low-turnover teams create turnovers only 
25 % of the time.

It seems that Shenzhen has the lowest 
efficacy rate in creating turnovers.
We next investigate when presses take place by dividing 
the match into 18 equal time intervals. For fair comparisons, 
we omit added time at the end of halves. In Figure 3, we 
provide a histogram of the number of traditional presses 
accumulated over all matches. We observe that matches 
begin with a slightly elevated level of pressing which dis-
sipates over the ﬁrst half.

This may be due to the energy 
available to teams at the beginning of matches. It may also
Figure 2: Barplots of the turnover percentage from traditional presses by CSL teams.

Figure 3: Histogram of the number of traditional presses according to the time of the match.
be due to home teams attempting to get an early lead and 
impress their fans. Overall, there is more pressing in the 
second half of matches. This may be explained by trailing 
teams needing to apply more pressure. We observe that 
the greatest amount of pressing occurs in the 45th to 50th 
minute.

This corresponds to the period following the half-
time break where energy is renewed, perhaps a change of 
tactics is introduced and perhaps a team has been encour-
aged by their manager. Recall that pressing requires a phys-
ical commitment and that half-time speaches may inspire a 
team.
We next investigate the frequency of traditional press-
ing throughout the match, classifying each pressing action 
as occurring while teams are either leading, tied, or trail-
ing.

In Figure 4, we produce a histogram of the number 
of presses per ﬁve-minute interval according to the above 
states. When teams are tied, pressing diminishes during 
each half. This may be explained by noting that teams are 
more cautious in tied games, and may not want to risk 
getting players caught upﬁeld while pressing. The results 
are less deﬁnitive and perhaps surprising when teams are 
either leading or trailing.

Overall, it seems that the pressing

rate in these states is mostly ﬂat. It could be that the lim-
ited pressing observed in the ﬁrst 10 min for both leading 
and trailing states are due to small sample sizes. Early in 
matches, there are seldom goals, and consequently there 
will be few early occasions where teams are either leading 
or trailing.
We also investigate whether home teams press more 
than road teams.

For traditional pressing, we calculate that 
home teams contribute to 52.71 % of the presses whereas 
road teams contribute to 47.29 % of the presses. Interest-
ingly, there is not a great difference in the overall pressing 
frequency between home and road teams. We therefore 
repeat the calculation for the ﬁrst 15 min of the match. In 
this case, home teams contribute to 54.13 % of the presses 
whereas road teams contribute to 45.87 % of the presses.

We 
hypothesize that home teams want to put on a good “show” 
for their supporters and begin pressing early in the match. 
Often the home team will score ﬁrst since the home team 
advantage is well established in football. At this stage, with 
the lead, there is no need for the home team to continue 
pressing, and this may explain the observed statistics. 
Of course, it is important to understand the outcomes 
from pressing.

In Figure 5, we present a heatmap visu-
alizing turnover density. Speciﬁcally, we highlight where 
traditional presses were initiated that eventually led to 
turnovers. We use kernel density estimation so that the 
darkest areas on the map indicate the zones with the highest 
frequency of these pressing initiation points. The heatmap 
shows that the corner areas furthest away from goal have 
the highest concentration of these presses.

It makes soccer
sense that such presses are often initiated near the sidelines 
since sidelines provide a boundary that restricts passing and 
movement. Also, it is interesting that the darkest regions are 
the least dangerous regions in the ﬁnal third from the point 
of view of the defending team. As expected, we also observe 
that there is near symmetry across the width of the ﬁeld. 
To provide more practical context, we counted how 
many turnovers resulted in a shot and found that about 
29.6 % of turnovers led to a shot.

2.4 Counter-pressing
Recall that counter-pressing is a tactic where a team 
immediately tries to regain possession of the ball in the 
ﬁnal third after losing it. Since counter-pressing has a 
different spatial structure than traditional pressing, and 
since counter-pressing has gained popularity, we analyze 
counter-pressing separately from traditional pressing. 
Table 3 presents descriptive statistics related to 
counter-pressing.

We observe monotonicity in the turnover 
rate (TO) with respect to closeout time t and intensity n. We 
also observe that most of the cells in Table 3 are greater 
than the corresponding cells in Table 2. This suggests that 
counter-pressing is associated with better outcomes than 
traditional pressing.
3 Pressing models
Although pressing is a fundamental strategy in soccer, the 
scientiﬁc literature on pressing is currently limited.

may be due to the challenges involved in (1) deﬁning a press, 
(2) collecting pressing data and (3) analyzing pressing data. 
In Section 2 of the paper, we have addressed the ﬁrst 
two challenges. In terms of analyzing pressing data, it is rec-
ognized that pressing data are complex. In Figure 6, we have 
divided the pressing region (i.e. the ﬁnal third of the ﬁeld) 
into six arbitrary regions labelled a − f .

These regions 
represent different functionalities with respect to pressing. 
By symmetry, regions a and c are similar, and regions d and f 
are similar. Region a represents a corner of the ﬁeld, region 
b represents the goal area, region d represents a sideline 
area, and region e represents a central area in front of goal. 
Now, if we were to consider ball movement involving these 
six regions over three passes, there would be 6 4 = 1, 296 
potential three-pass sequences.

Clearly, the cardinality and 
complexity of passing sequences pose a challenge for sta-
tistical analyses, even with an entire season of tracking 
data.
In Section 3.1 and Section 3.2, we introduce mod-
els based on assumptions that conform to football intu-
ition. These assumptions reduce the complexity of passing 
sequences. In turn, the proposed models permit analyses.
3.1 A Markov transition model
We can drastically reduce the dimensionality of passing 
sequences by introducing an intuitive Markov assumption.

Speciﬁcally, we assume that the movement of the ball (while 
pressed) from region j to region k is independent of the 
region where the ball was located prior to region j. Although 
this assumption simpliﬁes the modeling framework, it may 
not fully reﬂect realistic pressing behavior. Therefore, we 
assess the adequacy of the assumption in Section 3.1.2. 
In addition to the six regions of Figure 6 which allow 
us to describe ball movement during a press, we deﬁne the 
following three absorbing states which terminate a pressing 
sequence:
1.

BP – the press is broken
2. OB- the ball goes out of bounds by the pressed team
3. TO – the ball is turned over, giving possession to the 
pressing team
In our analysis, OB, TO and BP are pressing outcomes 
that are of tactical interest. We classify OB and TO as out-
comes which are favorable to the pressing team and BP as 
favourable to the pressed team. A broken press BP is deﬁned 
as a ball that is cleared beyond the ﬁnal third by the pressed 
team, or involves a stoppage where the pressed team gains 
possession.

We have grouped these two categories together 
to reduced complexity.
3.1.1 Transition matrices
For illustration, consider a press that begins in region a and 
involves the following three signiﬁcant movements prior to 
the press being broken: a → b → e → e → BP. Accordingly, 
we deﬁne a 6 × 9 Markov transition matrix where the 
described action results in an observation in each of the cells 
(a, b), (b, e), (e, e) and (e, BP).

Using all of the 7,596 traditional presses extracted from 
the 2019 CSL dataset as shown in Table 2, we produce the 
matrix of transitions in Table 4. Signiﬁcant movements are 
deﬁned as either a successful pass or a dribble of at least 2 m.

How-

The model was run with four independent chains, each with 
8,000 iterations. The ﬁrst 4,000 iterations of each chain were 
discarded as warm-up (burn-in).
3.2.1 Results
Under the above Bayesian framework, we are able to 
address pressing questions inferentially. Here, we illustrate 
the approach in the context of very hard presses (i.e. close-
out time t < 1.0 s) involving high intensity pressing (i.e.

n ≥ 4 players committed to the press). Note that this is 
a restricted dataset with smaller sample sizes. All other 
analyses in the preceding sections used the full dataset of 
traditional presses. The pressing strategy is of particular 
interest to teams that are looking to cause a turnover. We 
would like to know something about the success of pressing 
in this extreme pressing context.
In Table 9, we provide posterior probabilities of events 
related to turnovers based on the four initial pressing 
regions a, b, d, e.

Moreover, convergence diagnostics con-
ﬁrmed that all parameters had ̂R = 1.000 and effective sam-
ple sizes. HMC diagnostics showed no divergent transitions, 
no saturated tree depths, and good E-BFMI values. We 
observe that extreme pressing is a very effective strategy for 
turning over the ball. In particular, an extreme press which
begins in the central region b in front of goal results in a 
turnover 50 % of the time.

Presses originating in the regions 
a, d, e have slightly lower turnover rates. Other than region 
a, we see that turnover frequency dissipates as the number 
of transitions increases.
4 Discussion
To the best of our knowledge, this study presents the ﬁrst 
comprehensive framework for modelling traditional press-
ing in soccer using tracking data. With tracking data, the 
spatio-temporal aspect permits the identiﬁcation of the loca-
tion of all players at every instant during a match.

The meth-
ods utilized in our analyses include transition matrix theory 
based on a Markov assumption. In addition, a Bayesian 
model has been introduced which allows the incorporation 
of prior beliefs.
We have provided a deﬁnition of pressing which may 
be easily modiﬁed in future investigations. Presses have 
been classiﬁed as both hard and soft, indicating the com-
mittment to a particular press.

We have identiﬁed many 
observations concerning presses. These include the surpris-
ing result that pressing is is associated with better results 
when it is initiated in the goal area (i.e. region b). In future 
research, it would be good to attempt to replicate and extend 
the analyses for leagues beyond the Chinese Super League. 
While some of our ﬁndings may apply more generally, oth-
ers may depend on league-speciﬁc factors such as play-
ing style and team strategies.

Additional factors suggested 
by the exploratory data analysis, such as score differen-
tial, could also be incorporated to provide further insights. 
With sufficient data (or appropriate spatial smoothing), the 
Markov model could be extended to a continuous space 
framework, for example by accounting for the distance of 
a pass or player movement. Transition probabilities could 
be modelled to depend on other contextual factors, such as 
the number of steps in a sequence (n), the duration of the 
press (t), or the positioning of teammates and opponents.

Background
Tactical formation preferences in football are consid­
ered structural elements that directly influence not only 
the spatial arrangement of players on the pitch but also 
the flow of play, space distribution, and overall team 
strategy [23, 25].

In recent years, the impact of tacti­
cal formations on match outcomes has become more 
objectively measurable through advanced tracking tech­
nologies, positional data analytics, and artificial intelli­
gence-based systems [18, 23]. Nevertheless, comparative 
studies examining the diversity of formation preferences 
across Europe's elite leagues and their relationship with 
league standings remain limited [12].

Abstract
This study examines the distribution of tactical formations and their relationship with team success across the six 
major European football leagues (Premier League, La Liga, Serie A, Bundesliga, Ligue 1, and TFF Super League) 
during the 2023–2024 season.

A total of 2,132 matches and 4,038 formation data points were collected via OPTA 
Sportsdata and verified through fbref.com. The formations were grouped into eight main categories according to 
structural similarities. Statistical analyses included one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) and chi-square tests. The 
findings indicate that the 4–2-3–1 system was the most frequently used formation, while the 3–4-3 provided the 
highest average points per match.

The dominance of 4–2-3–1 was evident in the TFF Super League, whereas the 
3–4-3 was more common in the Bundesliga and Serie A, and the 4–4-2 was more prevalent in La Liga. Conversely, 
five-defender formations yielded lower average points and limited success. In conclusion, the effectiveness of 
tactical formations is not solely determined by their structural advantages but also by their alignment with league 
culture, player profiles, and managerial strategies.

These findings should be interpreted as a season-specific 
snapshot of formation usage patterns in the 2023–2024 season, rather than evidence of long-term tactical trends.

Tactical and performance analyses in football are con­
ducted through the systematic examination of events 
that occur consciously or automatically during match 
play.

These analyses constitute a fundamental source 
of data for coaches and sports scientists in interpreting 
and understanding player behaviors [22, 23]. The foot­
ball performance analysis literature generally seeks to 
explain the relationship between individual performance 
indicators and tactical organization [26]. Metrics such 
as high pressing, build-up play from the back, and duel 
success rates can be considered core components of the 
structural framework of tactical formations. Tactical 
formations represent fundamental strategic structures 
that determine not only players’ positional roles but also 
the playing philosophy of teams and leagues [16].

For 
coaches, these structures are regarded as one of the most 
functional tools for guiding or regulating player behav­
iors during match play [8]. In this context, In this context, 
tactical formations, which may be associated with team 
success in conjunction with multiple contextual factors, 
occupy a central position in contemporary football per­
formance analysis research [15].
In recent years, the increasing tempo of football has 
necessitated tactical evolution, leading to the develop­
ment of a more dynamic playing philosophy [31]. In 
modern football, congested fixture schedules and diver­
sifying opponent profiles have increased the frequency 
with which teams explore and experiment with different 
formations [11].

Within this context, although classical 
formations such as 4–2–3–1, 4–3-3, and 4–4-2 remain 
widely employed, it is well documented that formation 
preferences undergo year-on-year variations in accor­
dance with league dynamics [26]. Whether tactical for­
mations are associated with a team's success in league 
standings constitutes a significant and contemporary 
research area within football science [12].
The aims of this study are to: (a) identify the current 
tactical formations employed throughout the 2023–2024 
season across Europe's six major football leagues (Pre­
mier League, La Liga, Serie A, Bundesliga, Ligue 1, TFF 
Super League); (b) analyse the relationship between these 
formations and team success rankings; and (c) com­
paratively evaluate inter-league differences in formation 
preferences.

In this regard, the study aims to provide 
a strategic evidence base for both practitioners and the 
sport science literature.
Methods
Study design
This study is a retrospective descriptive investigation 
that examines the analytical design of tactical formations 
used in Europe’s top-tier football leagues from three fun­
damental perspectives. As part of the study procedure, 
the most up-to-date tactical formation models employed 
across the leagues were first identified.

Subsequently, the 
use of different tactical formations was analysed accord­
ing to teams’ final league rankings, and their associations 
with competitive success were examined. Finally, tacti­
cal formations were compared across leagues to identify 
inter-league differences [25].
Samples
Within the scope of this research, all data were obtained 
from matches played during the 2023–2024 season 
across six major football leagues in Europe.

The leagues 
included in the study were England (Premier League), 
Germany (Bundesliga), Spain (La Liga), France (Ligue 
1), Italy (Serie A), and Türkiye (TFF Super League). For 
each of the 2,132 matches played in total, both competing 
teams were considered as separate observational units. 
Furthermore, with the recording of in-match tactical 
changes, a total of 4,038 observations were included in 
the study.

To ensure methodological consistency, teams 
that played with ten players due to a red card dismissal 
for more than 45 min of match time, as well as instances 
where any identified tactical formation was employed 
for fewer than 15  min during a match, were excluded 
from the analysis. Finally, goalkeepers were not included 
within the analytical scope during the identification and 
reporting of tactical formations.

To analyse the relationship between formation pref­
erences and team success levels across leagues, teams 
were categorised according to success tiers. Team suc­
cess levels were classified based on each league's UEFA 
competition qualification quota and the league structures 
established at the end of the season. This classification 
approach is grounded in UEFA's club coefficient ranking 
system and methodological frameworks proposed in the 
existing literature [3].

Consequently, the influence of for­
mation utilisation preferences on success within the con­
text of teams' domestic league performance was rendered 
analytically examinable.
Team success classification by league was defined as 
follows:
England—Premier League: Teams ranked 1–4 were 
classified as UEFA Champions League qualifiers; 
teams ranked 5–7 as UEFA Europa and Conference 
League qualifiers; teams ranked 8–17 as mid-table 
teams; and teams ranked 18–20 as relegated teams.

Data collection (sources)
The tactical formation data analysed in this study were 
collected by OPTA Sportsdata and subsequently cross-
validated using the publicly available football statistics 
platform fbref.com. This platform provides detailed 
information for each match, including starting forma­
tions, player positions, and technical-tactical actions. 
A review of the literature indicates that OPTA data are 
widely used in football research and that high inter-oper­
ator reliability in data coding procedures has been consis­
tently reported in scientific studies [14].

League standings 
were obtained from the official websites of the respective 
national football federations.
According to the data provided by OPTA Sportsdata 
and the fbref.com platform, 18 different tactical forma­
tions employed by teams during the 2023–2024 sea­
son were recorded. However, to enable more systematic 
analysis and enhance interpretive power, these forma­
tions were grouped into eight main formation categories 
based on their widely recognised structural similarities.

During the classification process, the evaluation and 
matching of formation structures were interpreted and 
categorised under the guidance of coaches holding UEFA 
A and B licences as well as match and performance analy­
sis certifications. Similarly, Borrie et al. [2] utilised UEFA 
A-licensed coaches in the evaluation of tactical patterns 
within football analysis research. Through this approach, 
the systematic dataset was substantiated in terms of both 
technical accuracy and interpretive reliability.

Statistical analysis
IBM SPSS Statistics version 25 (IBM SPSS Inc., Chicago, 
IL, USA) and Microsoft Excel 2010 were used for the 
statistical analysis of the data obtained from the study. 
The Kolmogorov–Smirnov test was applied to assess the 
normality of data distribution. One-way analysis of vari­
ance (ANOVA) was used to compare mean differences 
in points per match across leagues and tactical forma­
tion groups.

The chi-square test of independence was 
employed to examine differences in the distribution of 
categorical formation variables across leagues. Statistical 
significance was set at p < 0.05.

Discussion
This study provides a descriptive overview of tactical for­
mation usage across Europe’s top-tier leagues during the 
2023–2024 season and examines their associations with 
team success indicators. Overall, formation distributions 
differed across leagues, and points-per-match values var­
ied across formation groups. In the points-per-match 
comparisons (Table 4), the 3–5-2 group showed the high­
est mean value, whereas the 5–3-2 group showed the 
lowest mean value; however, these comparisons should 
be interpreted cautiously due to small sample sizes in 
some formation categories and the small-to-moderate 
effect size (η2 = 0.054).

Collectively, the findings should 
be interpreted as season-specific associations rather 
than evidence of causal effects. Previous studies have 
described tactical characteristics of three-defender sys­
tems such as the 3–5-2 formation, particularly in rela­
tion to midfield structure and transitional play [6, 21]. 
In the overall formation-level descriptive analysis of the 
present study (Table  1), the 3–5-2 formation showed a 
relatively lower average points value (x̄ = 0.99).

However, 
when examined at the team-level through the ANOVA 
comparison (Table 4), this formation displayed the high­
est mean points-per-match value. This difference reflects 
variations between analytical levels rather than contra­
dictory findings and should be interpreted cautiously 
given the limited number of observations for this for­
mation group. Therefore, the current results should be 
considered as season-specific associations rather than 
definitive performance implications.

One possible explanation for this discrepancy may be 
the limited availability of elite-level wing-back players 
capable of performing effectively in both defensive and 
offensive phases of play [20, 24]. Considering that these 
players must possess high levels of physical endurance 
and tactical awareness, the translation of the 3–5-2 for­
mation’s potential onto the pitch may depend not only on 
formation preference but also on overall squad quality.

Memmert et al. [16], in their analyses at the UEFA Cham­
pions League level, reported that formations incorporat­
ing a three-player defensive line demonstrated greater 
consistency across physical and technical dimensions, 
thereby reducing performance fluctuations throughout a 
season. Although these findings support the theoretical 
advantages of the 3–5-2 formation, they also suggest that 
several contextual limitations may influence how these 
advantages are realized in larger datasets, as observed 
in the present study.

Additionally, Leontijević et al. [13] 
noted that the successful implementation of the 3–5-2 
formation requires high levels of player fitness and tac­
tical adaptability and has been more commonly adopted 
in defence-oriented leagues such as Serie A. In our study, 
the relatively higher preference rate of the 3–5-2 forma­
tion in Serie A aligns with this defensive tradition. From 
a broader tactical perspective, the evolution of European 
football has contributed to the transformation of clas­
sical systems such as the 3–5-2 into more flexible and 
attack-oriented structures.

González-Ródenas et al. [10] 
reported an increase in the use of the 3–5-2 formation 
in La Liga and emphasized its capacity to provide posi­
tional variability compared with more attack-oriented 
structures such as the 4–2–3–1 and 4–4-2. However, 
the findings of the present study suggest that, within the 
examined season, this tactical evolution may be more 
closely associated with a shift toward the 3–4-3 forma­
tion. Across the 2023–2024 season, the 3–4-3 forma­
tion was frequently observed and was associated with 
relatively high points-per-match values in the formation-
level descriptive analysis (Table 1; x̄ = 1.81).

This pattern 
was also evident in certain league contexts, suggesting 
that the formation appeared across different competitive 
environments within the present sample. The structural 
emphasis on effective pitch width in this formation has 
been noted in previous research as potentially facilitating 
the exploitation of spaces within defensive lines [9, 27]. 
However, given the observational design and the single-
season scope of the study, these findings should be inter­
preted as descriptive associations rather than evidence of 
a consistent performance advantage across leagues.

The 4–3-3 formation was among the commonly used 
systems in the present dataset and showed relatively high 
points-per-match values (Table  4; x̄ = 1.53). Although 
the formation was less preferred in some leagues (e.g., 
Bundesliga and the TFF Super League), it appeared more 
frequently among higher-ranked teams, suggesting that 
its use may reflect contextual and tactical preferences 
rather than a direct performance effect.

Therefore, these 
observations should be interpreted as descriptive, sea­
son-specific associations within the current sample.
The 4–5-1 formation appeared less frequently across 
the six leagues but showed mid-range points-per-match 
values within the present dataset. Previous literature 
suggests that the five-midfielder structure may enhance 
ball possession and function as a balancing element 
during attacking–defensive transitions [29].

Differ­
ences observed between leagues suggest that its use may 
depend on contextual tactical preferences rather than 
indicating a consistent performance advantage. Accord­
ingly, these findings should be interpreted as descriptive, 
season-specific associations rather than causal effects.

The 4–2–3–1 formation is widely recognised in modern 
football due to its structural balance between defensive 
organisation and attacking flexibility [4, 5]. In the present 
study, this formation was the most frequently employed 
system across the six leagues and was associated with 
relatively higher mean points per match (x̄ = 1.44) within 
the 2023–2024 season.

Previous research has suggested 
that formations of this type may support ball circula­
tion, transition play, and positional versatility in high-
tempo competitive environments [1, 19, 32]. In line with 
these descriptions, teams employing the 4–2–3–1 in our 
sample accumulated points above both the overall league 
average and relegation-zone teams,however, these obser­
vations should be interpreted as season-specific associa­
tions rather than evidence of a direct performance effect. 
Overall, the findings indicate that the widespread use of 
the 4–2–3–1 formation may reflect its tactical adaptabil­
ity across different league contexts within this observa­
tional dataset.

The 4–4-2 formation remains one of the classical tac­
tical structures in football, offering a compact balance 
between defensive organisation and attacking support [5, 
30]. In the present study, this formation ranked among 
the commonly used systems and showed relatively high 
mean points-per-match values (x̄ = 1.58). Although previ­
ous literature has described structural advantages related 
to simplicity and positional clarity, the findings of this 
study should be interpreted as descriptive associations 
rather than evidence of a direct performance benefit.

Overall, the continued use of the 4–4-2 formation across 
leagues may reflect its tactical familiarity and adaptability 
within different competitive contexts.
The 5–3-2 formation represents a defensively oriented 
structure that has been described in the literature as sup­
porting compact organisation and transition play [5, 16]. 
In the present study, this formation appeared less fre­
quently across leagues and demonstrated comparatively 
lower mean points-per-match values (x̄ = 1.29).

While 
contextual differences between leagues may influence 
formation preferences, the current findings should be 
interpreted as descriptive season-specific observations 
rather than general performance implications. The 5–4-1 
formation is commonly described as a defensively com­
pact structure that prioritises organisation and stability, 
while potentially limiting attacking output due to the 
single-forward configuration [5, 28].

In the present study, 
the 5–4-1 formation was among the least frequently 
observed systems across the six leagues and showed com­
paratively low mean points per match (x̄ = 1.11). It was 
more frequently used in the Premier League and Serie 
A than in leagues such as the Super League, Bundesliga, 
and La Liga, suggesting that league context may influ­
ence the practical deployment of this formation.

Over­
all, these findings should be interpreted as descriptive, 
season-specific associations rather than evidence of con­
sistent performance effects.
Limitations
The findings of this study should be interpreted within 
the context of several methodological and contextual lim­
itations. Firstly, data on tactical formations were derived 
exclusively from teams’ starting line-ups and the forma­
tions predominantly used throughout matches.

Dynamic 
formational transitions during play, micro-tactical 
adjustments, and momentary role changes were excluded 
from the scope of analysis. Moreover, potential variables 
that may influence the effectiveness of formations, such 
as player profiles, coaches’ strategic preferences, and con­
textual match characteristics (e.g., match importance, 
home–away status, and environmental conditions), were 
not incorporated into the analytical framework.

The 
restriction of data to a single season limits the evaluation 
of formational trends through long-term comparisons. 
Additionally, the relatively small sample size for certain 
tactical formations should be considered as a factor that 
may constrain the generalisability of the obtained results.
For future studies, it is recommended that the influence 
of tactical formations on success not be evaluated solely 
through match outcomes.

Analysis in conjunction with 
broader performance indicators such as ball possession 
percentage, expected goals (xG), passing networks, and 
in-match positional stability is recommended. Further­
more, the effectiveness of each formation across differ­
ent match scenarios (e.g., situations of score advantage, 
draws, and deficits) requires comparative examination. 
Such examination would provide a stronger evidence 
base for managers' decision-making processes.

Conclusion
This study provided a comparative evaluation of tacti­
cal formations by examining 4,038 formations employed 
across a total of 2,132 matches during the 2023–2024 
season in six top-tier European football leagues, focus­
ing on formation preference rates and average points per 
match. The findings demonstrate that tactical formations 
are directly associated with match success and that this 
relationship varies according to the structural, cultural, 
and strategic characteristics of each league. The obser­
vation that formations such as 5–4-1 and 5–3-2, which 
are favourably evaluated in the literature for defensive 
stability and transition play, exhibited low mean points 
and limited preference rates in the analysed leagues indi­
cates that formation success depends not only on struc­
tural advantages but also on contextual implementation 
proficiency.

In contrast, attack-oriented formations that 
support transition play and wide area utilisation (such as 
4–3-3 and 3–4-3) stood out with both higher mean points 
and more widespread preference rates. In particular, the

finding that the 4–2–3–1 formation was the most fre­

in the study and ranked in the upper positions in terms 
of average points reflects modern football's requirement 
for defensive-attacking balance. Specifically in the Super 
League, the high preference rate for the 4–2–3–1 and the 
relatively successful mean points of the 4–4-2 were note­
worthy, whilst formations based on five-defender struc­
tures were observed to remain limited with low success 
rates.

These results demonstrate that the effectiveness of 
tactical formations depends not only on the structural 
theoretical advantages of the formation but also on align­
ment with league dynamics, player profiles, and tactical 
strategies.

Multivariate analysis of indirect free kick in the FIFA World Cup 2014 
 
Rubén Maneiro Dios1*, José Luis Losada López2, Claudio Alberto Casal Sanjurjo3 and Antonio Ardá Suárez4 
 
1 Universidad Pontificia de Salamanca, Salamanca (Spain).

2 Universidad de Barcelona, Barcelona (Spain). 
3 Universidad Católica de Valencia “San Vicente Mártir”, Valencia (Spain). 
4 Universidad de A Coruña, A Coruña (Spain). 
 
Título: Análisis multivariante del tiro libre indirecto en la Copa del Mundo 
de la FIFA 2014. 
Resumen: Los tiros libres indirectos son situaciones que se producen con 
regularidad durante los partidos de fútbol, siendo acciones potencialmente 
trascendentales en el resultado final de los partidos.

Los objetivos de este 
estudio fueron determinar la efectividad de estas acciones, identificar las va-
riables asociadas con el éxito y proponer un modelo de tiro libre indirecto 
exitoso.  
Fueron codificados y analizados 506 tiros libres indirectos registrados en 
los 64 partidos de la FIFA World Cup Brasil 2014, se llevaron a cabo análi-
sis univariados, bivariados (Ji-Cuadrado) y multivariados (regresión logística 
binaria), los resultados indican una baja eficacia en el remate, remate entre 
los tres palos y el gol en este tipo de acciones.

En cambio, el 89% de los go-
les con procedencia en un tiro libre indirecto han contribuido a sumar pun-
tos en el resultado final de los partidos. La organización ofensiva, basada en 
maniobras de creación y ocupación de espacios, y la intervención de hasta 4 
jugadores, son variables que se han revelado como moduladoras de la efica-
cia. Sin duda, estos enunciados podrían suponer un punto de partida para 
dotar a entrenadores de nuevas herramientas tácticas con el fin de dotar de 
un perfil más eficaz en este tipo de acciones.

Palabras clave: Regresión logística; metodología observacional; fútbol; sa-
que de esquina. 
 
Abstract: Indirect free kicks are relatively common in soccer and have the 
potential to change the outcome of a match. The aim of this study was to 
determine the effectiveness of these kicks, to identify variables associated 
with success, and propose a model for optimal execution.  
We analyzed and coded 506 indirect free kicks taken in 64 matches during 
the FIFA 2014 World Cup in Brazil and conducted univariate, bivariate 
(chi-square), and multivariate (binary logistic regression) analyses.

Our re-
sults show very low success rates in terms of shots, shots between the 
posts, and goals. Nevertheless, 89% of goals scored from indirect free kicks 
led to the teams gaining valuable points. Determinants of success included 
a dynamic attack based on the creation and occupation of spaces and the 
intervention of up to four attackers. Our findings offer an interesting start-
ing point for trainers to build on tactical strategies designed to improve 
free-kick performance.

Key words: Logistic Regression; observational methodology; soccer; cor-
ner. 
 
Introduction 
 
The search for success factors, i.e., factors directly associat-
ed with winning, forms a key part of research in soccer and 
indeed sport in general. The identification thus of possible 
routes to victory, supported by solid evidence, should be a 
priority for sports researchers within their ultimate search 
for an explanation of everything.

The subsequent dissemina-
tion of findings in a format that is accessible to trainers and 
players alike could have a direct impact on the overall per-
formance of individuals and teams.  
The expression “less talk and more evidence” would ap-
pear to be particularly pertinent in soccer, where everyone 
has opinions and theories about what actually happens on 
the pitch. This speculative approach, however, is a far cry 
from the scientific rigor required to answer the numerous 
questions that arise in this intricate sport científico (Harris y 
Reilly, 1988).

It is here where researchers’ strive for rigor be-
comes relevant, as a systematic, rigorous analysis can help to 
find order in the seeming chaos of a soccer match through 
the identification of patterns and the assignment of meaning 
to the complex interactions that occur.  
Within this strive for a greater understanding of the in-
tricacies of soccer and a reduction of the element of chance,

the scientific community has produced extensive research on 
the two main components of play: dynamic or open play sit-
uations, which account for 60% to 70% of all actions in a 
match (McGarry, Anderson, Wallace, Hughes y Franks, 
2002), and static or dead ball situations, which account for 
the remaining 30% to 40% (Maneiro, 2014; Yiannakos y 
Armatas, 2006).

Of the many performance indicators that have been ana-
lyzed in situations of open play (Mackenzie & Cushion, 
2012), ball possession is perhaps one of the most widely 
studied. Several retrospective studies have found a direct 
link between possession and winning (Bloomfield, Polman, 
& O´Donoghue, 2005; Hughes & Franks, 2005 and Jones, 
James, & Mellalieu, 2004).  
Studies of static play have analyzed how goal scoring and 
match outcomes are influenced by performance in set plays 
or dead-ball situations.

According to empirical work by 
Yiannakos and Armatas (2006) and Armatas and Yiannakos 
(2010), approximately one-third of all goals scored in the 
FIFA World Cup and the UEFA European Championship 
are, directly or indirectly, a result of set plays. This is perti-
nent, as the number of goals scored per match has reached 
an all-time low and has shown no signs of increasing in re-
cent years (see Figure 1).

This stagnation can largely be ex-
plained by greater defensive organization and intensity and 
more rigorous implementation of tactical planning. Soccer is 
in general a low-scoring sport, unlike basketball or handball, 
for example, and the lack of goals could potentially detract

Based on our review of the literature, the most effective 
set plays in terms of goal scoring are penalty kicks (Armatas, 
Yiannakos, Papadopoulou, & Galazoulas, 2007), followed by 
indirect free kicks and corner kicks, although goals resulting 
from direct free kicks appear to be on the rise (Njororai, 
2013). Throw-ins, goal kicks, and kickoffs, by contrast, are 
associated with low scoring rates.

An estimated 70% to 85% of penalty kicks taken by pro-
fessional soccer players result in a goal (Jordet, Hartman, 
Visscher, & Lemmink, 2007; McGarry & Franks, 2000). Pa-
lacios-Huerta (2003), on analyzing 1417 penalty kicks, con-
cluded that to be a highly effective penalty taker, players 
need to learn to shoot into different areas of the goal. In a 
later study, Bar-Eli and Azar (2009), found that penalty kicks 
were more likely to be successful (100% so) if they were 
aimed at the upper two corners of the goal.

Penalty shoot-outs have also been analyzed. In a large 
study of 269 penalty shoot-outs consisting of 2820 penalty 
kicks, Apesteguia and Palacios-Huerta (2010) found that 
outcome was influenced by kicking order (determined by a 
coin toss), with teams who took the first kick having a 60% 
chance of winning the shoot-out. 
More recent empirical studies have provided interesting 
insights into corner kick performance.

Although corner 
kicks are associated with a very low goal rate (around 2% ac-
cording to Schmicker, 2013), the goals they produce can de-
cide the outcome of the match in 76% of cases (Casal, 
Maneiro, Ardá, Losada & Rial, 2015). With respect to tactics, 
two recent studies (Casal, Losada, Maneiro, & Ardá, in press; 
Sainz de Baranda & López-Riquelme, 2012) have shown that 
the score of the match at the moment of a corner kick can 
influence the outcome and suggested that the fastest way to 
a create a scoring opportunity is to put the ball immediately 
into play and reach the shooting area using simple, straight-
forward attacking tactics.

The most effective direct free kicks appear to be kicks 
taken from central areas of the pitch, kicks taken with the 
opposite foot to the side of the pitch (Carling, Williams, & 
Reilly, 2005), and kicks aimed at the upper corners of the 
goal (Alcock, 2010). Although there is a lack of consensus 
on the success rates of direct free kicks, in general, they ap-
pear to be surprisingly ineffective, with just 8%, in the best 
of cases, resulting in a goal (Silva, 2011).

Interestingly, 
Savelsbergh, Cañal-Bruland, and van der Kamp (2012) de-
signed training protocols aimed at improving free-kick per-
formance in soccer and found that an error-reduction proto-
col with increasing task difficulty resulted in a lasting im-
provement in results.  
Finally, from our review of the literature, it would seem 
that very few empirical studies have analyzed indirect free 
kicks.

One of the first studies to analyze these kicks, con-
ducted by Van Meerbeek, Van Gool, and Bollens (1988), an-
alyzed free kicks taken at the 1986 World Cup in Mexico. 
They described an average of 9.6 indirect free kicks per 
match and reported that the majority had come from offside 
situations. Indirect free kicks are relatively ineffective, with 
just 14% resulting in a shot (Mara, Weeler, & Lyons, 2012) 
and 3% resulting in a goal.

In a recent study by our group, 
we found that an offensive set-up in which the ball was 
passed along the ground between three or four players be-

Findings such as the above highlight the importance of

The 
overall aim of this empirical study was to analyze the effec-
tiveness of indirect free kicks in elite soccer within the con-
text of different factors of play. We had three specific objec-
tives: to objectively analyze the effectiveness of these kicks, 
to identify potential determinants of success, and to create 
explanatory models to guide the work of trainers and play-
ers.  
 
Method 
 
Sample 
 
We studied 506 indirect free kicks taken during the 64 
matches of the FIFA World Cup in Brazil 2014.

We chose 
this competition in order to control for the main situational 
variables found to influence tactical/strategic behavior in 
soccer (Jones, James, & Mellalieu, 2004; Lago & Martín, 
2007; O´Donoghue & Tenga, 2001; Sasaki, Nevill, & Reilly, 
1999; Shaw & O´Donoghue, 2004; Tucker, Mellalieu, James, 
& Taylor, 2005), namely, venue (all the matches were played 
on a neutral pitch), level of the teams (matches played by 
top national teams), and match status (e.g., winning, 
drawing, or losing) at the time of the kick.

We only included 
free kicks that involved four or fewer passes before a shot 
was taken (Bate, 1988).  
 
Instruments 
 
We used a previously described ad hoc observation in-
strument comprising a combination of field formats and cat-
egory systems (Table 1). The full definitions of the catego-
ries can be consulted in the study describing the design of 
the instrument (Casal et al. 2014).

Procedure 
 
The study design falls into quadrant IV (follow-
up/nomothetic/multidimensional) of the observational 
methodology models described by Anguera, Blanco, and 
Losada (2001).  
Once all the relevant sequences of play had been extract-
ed from public video footage of the matches, four observers 
applied the observation instrument to code all events and

behaviors. The observers are all Doctors in Physical Activity 
and Sports Sciences, experts in observational methodology, 
and national soccer trainers. In addition, they were specifi-
cally trained for the purpose of the study during eight ses-
sions using the consensus agreement method described by 
Anguera (1990), in which events and behaviors are coded 
only when there is agreement between the observers.

The 
data were recorded and coded in the LINCE software pro-
gram (Gabin, Camerino, Anguera, & Castañer, 2012).  
The reliability of the resulting datasets was assessed by 
calculating interobserver agreement using Cohen’s kappa 
statistic for each of the criteria in the observation instru-
ment. Overall agreement was 0.94, which, according to the 
scale of Fleiss, Levin, and Paik (2003), can be considered 
very good.

We performed three types of analysis—a descriptive or 
univariate analysis, a comparative or bivariate analysis, and 
an explanatory or multivariate analysis. The descriptive anal-
ysis provided information on the number of indirect free 
kicks taken, on how these kicks were taken, and on how 
successful they were. In our bivariate analysis, we created 
different contingency tables (with chi-square tests and asso-
ciation measures) to identify variables potentially associated 
with successful outcomes.

Finally, we used multivariate lo-
gistic regression to identify significant predictors of success-
ful free kicks. Success was defined as an indirect free kick 
that resulted in one of the following: a shot (outside the 
posts), a shot between the posts, or a goal.  
Three success criteria have been taken into account: if a 
shot is produced, regardless of whether it is aimed at goal or 
not; if the shot is directed between the goal posts; and if the 
shot gets a goal.

Results 
 
A total of 1893 direct and indirect free kicks were taken in 
the 64 matches played at the FIFA 2014 World Cup in Bra-
zil. This corresponds to a mean of 29.57 kicks per match. Of 
these 1893 kicks, 506 met the inclusion criteria for the study. 
Almost three-quarters (73.3%) of the free kicks were direct 
kicks, while the remaining 26.7% were indirect kicks or di-
rect kicks taken as if they were indirect kicks.

This corre-
sponded to an average of 7.9 indirect free kicks per match. 
Although these kicks produced eight specific goal-scoring 
opportunities per match, they were overall very ineffective 
(Figure 3), as only 1.8% ended in a goal, 10% ended in a 
shot between the posts, and 22.1% ended in a shot. This 
lack of effectiveness is even more patent if we consider that 
each team failed to take advantage of four specific opportu-
nities to score and change the result of each match.

Empirically, our results show that almost five indirect 
free kicks taken with the purpose of scoring a goal are need-
ed to produce a shot, while 10 are needed to produce a shot 
between the posts, and 56 are needed to actually score a 
goal.  
Despite their overall ineffectiveness, however, goals re-
sulting from indirect free kicks had a decisive impact on the 
final outcome of matches, as eight (89%) of the nine goals 
scored helped the teams to gain valuable points (Figure 4).

Multivariate analysis 
 
For the third objective of the study, we performed sev-
eral multivariate logistic regression analyses to identify mod-
els that would help to explain or predict the effectiveness of 
indirect free kicks in elite soccer. The dependent variables, 
all dichotomous, were shot, shot between the posts, and 
goal, while the explanatory variables, or predictors, were var-
iables significantly associated with the three dichotomous 
variables in the bivariate analysis (five variables for shot and 
shot between the posts and four variables for goal).

The 
models were built using stepwise selection based on the 
Wald test. 
For the criterion shot (Table 5), the probability of a suc-
cessful outcome was 10.055 higher when the indirect free 
kick was defended by between one and four players rather 
than seven or more. A similar four-fold increase was ob-
served when five or six defenders were used. In the case of 
ball delivery, the likelihood of a shot resulting from an indi-
rect free kick was reduced by a factor of 0.514 when the ball 
was delivered to the shooting area using several players ra-
ther than directly. Similarly, a shot was 0.111 times less likely 
when the ball was delivered along than ground rather than 
through the air, and 0.003 times less likely when the number 
of attackers intervening in the kick was one or two rather 
than three or four. Finally, a static attack was 0.334 times 
less likely than a dynamic attack to result in a shot from an 
indirect free kick.

The Hosmer-Lemeshow and Nagelkerke R2 tests both 
showed a good fit for the model, with respective scores of 
0.797 and 0.650.

Discussion 
 
This study had three separate yet complementary objectives. 
The first was to provide empirical evidence on the effective-
ness of indirect free kicks in elite soccer, using data from the 
2014 World Cup in Brazil. The second objective was to 
identify variables or tactical elements with a possible influ-
ence on free-kick performance, and the third objective was 
to develop multivariate models to explain and/or predict the 
effectiveness of indirect free kicks.

We registered 1893 direct and indirect free kicks in the 
64 matches analyzed. This corresponds to a mean of 29.6 
kicks per match, which is similar to figures reported by 
Siegle and Lames (2012) and Wallace and Norton (2014). 
Just over a quarter of these kicks (n=506) were regular indi-
rect kicks or direct kicks taken as if they were indirect kicks. 
Again, this proportion is similar to rates reported by Van 
Meerbeek, Van Gool, and Bollens (1988) and by Casal et al.

(2014). 
The average number of indirect free kicks taken per 
match—eight—is similar to that reported by Silva (2011) 
and Casal et al. (2014), but considerably lower than that re-
ported by Carling et al. (2005) (12 kicks per match). 
One of the first observations to emerge from our data is 
that despite their relative frequency, indirect free kicks are 
largely ineffective. Just 1.8% of the 506 kicks led to a goal, 
and only 22.1% resulted in a shot.

This last rate is higher 
than that reported by Mara, Weeler, and Lyons (2012) and 
similar to that reported by Maneiro (2014). 
The overall ineffectiveness of indirect free kicks, howev-
er, contrasts sharply with the impact that goals resulting 
from these kicks have on the final outcome of matches. Our 
data show that practically nine of every ten goals scored 
from an indirect free kick lead to a win or a draw.

As found 
in a previous study by our group (Casal et al., 2014) goals 
scored from free kicks are few are far between but they can 
be decisive. 
Like Maneiro (2014), we believe that the multiple, com-
plex factors underlying free-kick situations are partly respon-
sible for this overall lack of effectiveness, but we also believe 
that that insufficient practise and planning have a role. It is 
not uncommon to see free kicks taken with what appears to 
be little foresight or consideration of the immediate context.

Our results suggest that free kicks should form part of week-
ly training programmes designed to build tactics that offer 
an alternative to on-the-spot decisions taken during match 
situations.   
Our bivariate investigation of variables potentially asso-
ciated with free kick success recurring variables: the number 
of attackers that intervene in the sequence leading up a shot 
following an indirect free kick and the organization of the at-
tack.

With just one exception—number of defenders—all the 
variables significantly associated with either a shot or a shot 
between the posts were related to offensive play (delivery 
and path of the ball, number of attackers, and offensive or-
ganization). This observation supports previous findings by 
our team (Casal et al., 2015), and adds strength to the idea 
that indirect free kicks should be practised in order to re-
duce the element of chance and uncertainty by building pat-
terns and skills designed to achieve optimal execution.

The variables found to be associated with goals scored 
from indirect free kicks again show that the key to success 
would appear to lie in simplicity and tactical refinement, 
which is quite the opposite to what is typically seen in free-
kick situations. Like Maneiro (2014), however, we also found 
that the position of the free kick influences the likelihood of 
scoring.  
Although statistically, the results of our multiple logistic 
regression analysis are modest in their predictive ability, at 
an applied level, they are very interesting, as they could help 
to increase the overall effectiveness of indirect free kicks.

We found that the likelihood of an indirect free kick 
ending in a shot increased significantly when the ball was 
sent directly to the shooting area, with a pass through the 
air, within a dynamically organized attack involving three to 
four attackers and four defenders at the most. Again, our re-
sults support previous findings by our group that indirect 
free kicks are more effective when the attackers move 
around the shooting area and when several players intervene 
in the sequence leading up to the shot (Casal et al., 2014).

A 
novel finding of the present study, however, is that it is im-
portant to send the ball to the shooting area rapidly and 
through the air at some point. These differences can proba-
bly be explained by the fact that while dynamic play does not 
vary significantly from one World Cup to another (Castella-
no, Perea, & Hernández Mendo, 2008; Castellano, Perea y 
Blanco-Villaseñor, 2007), set play does, as it is more likely to 
be influenced by predefined strategies and positional tactics

aimed at minimizing interaction with the defense. These ac-
tions, however, can be easily studied and their effects neu-
tralized, highlighting the importance of constant innovation 
and renewal in set-play situations.

We also found that the probability of an indirect free 
kick ending in a shot between the posts was significantly in-
creased by organizing the attack dynamically and passing the 
ball through the air. This observation indicates that it is not 
enough to simply deliver the ball to the shooting area, but to 
ensure that the awaiting attackers vary their positions, by 
moving around, feinting, and pulling/pushing to create 
space (Ardá, Maneiro, Rial, Losada, & Casal, 2014).

Finally, we observed that indirect free kicks resulted in 
more goals when the defending team was playing zone de-
fense, suggesting that in these situations the attacking team 
should position more players in the immediate defensive ar-
ea to create uncertainty. 
The results of this empirical study are consistent with 
previous findings by Casal et al. (2014) and Maneiro (2014) 
and highlight again the importance of elaborate moves, prior 
practice, and targeted rather than random delivery of the ball 
to the shooting area.

The fact that teams study each other’s 
strategies also suggests that these actions should be as crea-
tive and as unpredictable as possible. 
 
Conclusions 
 
The main conclusions that can be drawn from our study are  
1) Indirect free kicks are relatively common in elite soccer.  
2) Overall, they are very ineffective, as four free kicks are 
needed to produce a shot, 12 to produce a shot between 
the posts, and 56 to produce a goal.

3) The way of taking indirect free kicks has evolved from 
the 2010 World Cup to the 2014 World Cup. 
4) An indirect free kick is more likely to result in a shot or a 
shot between the posts when the attacking side organizes 
itself dynamically and when three or four players are in-
volved in the sequence leading up to the shot.  
 
Practical applications  
 
Our study has several practical applications as our findings 
could help trainers and players to improve both the efficien-
cy and effectiveness of indirect free kicks by providing them 
with new tools and strategies with immediate application.

Considering the relative frequency of these set plays in elite 
soccer, improved free-kick performance is likely to increase 
scoring opportunities and make the game more attractive. 
By being familiar with factors that can help to convert an 
indirect free kick into a clear scoring opportunity, trainers 
will be able to propose alternatives to traditional, yet ineffec-
tive, tactics based on direct airborne passes from the taker of 
the free kick.

And logically, they will be able to incorporate 
these new models into regular training sessions.  
Finally, the fact that we analyzed interactions between 
variables will also help trainers to build a richer repertoire of 
strategies designed to improve their team’s performance 
both in terms of indirect free kicks and overall.

The use of player tracking data to analyze
defensive play in professional soccer - A
scoping review
Leander Forcher1
, Stefan Altmann1,3, Leon Forcher1,2,
Darko Jekauc1 and Matthias Kempe4
Abstract
The analysis of tracking data in tactical game analysis is a topic of rising interest, as more detailed insights into performance
structure in soccer can be obtained compared to traditional (e.g. notational) analyzes.

Compared to the variety and detailed
analyzes of offensive play, the number of studies analyzing the defensive play is low. However, in recent years, an increasing
number of studies investigating defensive play have been published, so it seems useful to provide an overview of the current
state of research in this area. Therefore, this study aims to identify the approaches that have been used to analyze the defen-
sive play in professional soccer using player tracking data and to reveal the ﬁndings on successful defensive play.

A systematic
literature search of electronic databases (PubMed (n = 604), Web of Science (n = 593), and SPORTDiscuss (n = 872)) was
conducted according to the PRISMA extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR). Studies that were included used tracking
data of professional adult male soccer and analyzed defensive play. The result is a total of 23 studies that were analyzed in
detail using the standardized quality assessment checklist for systematic reviews in sports science.

The synthesis of results
was carried out descriptively by organizing the results into different levels of tactical play (individual level, group level, team
level). All included studies were of good methodological quality. The approaches to investigate defensive play using tracking
data are highly heterogeneous (e.g. analysis of defensive pressure, analysis of synchronization, behavioral analyzes, ball recov-
eries).

Successful defensive play is characterized by high pressure at the individual level, by high inter-team and intra-team
synchronization and balanced defense at the group level, and by a compact coordinated organization at the team level. By
summarizing the state of research on defensive play in soccer using sophisticated analysis approaches that showcase the pos-
sibilities of tracking data, this study provides an important foundation for future research in this area.
Keywords
Association football, performance indicators, tactical game analysis
Highlights
• The approaches to analyze defensive play in soccer using
tracking data are highly heterogenous.

• Most promising approaches to analyze defensive play are
the analysis of defensive pressure (at the individual level)
and the quantiﬁcation of compact organization (at the
group level).
• Successful defensive play is characterized by high defen-
sive pressure (at the individual level), inter-team and
intra-team
synchronization
as
well
as
a
balanced
defense (at the group level), and the contraction of organ-
ization (at the team level).

Introduction
Match analysis in soccer has been in the focus of interest for
the scientiﬁc community and coaches for more than seventy
years.1 The majority of publications in science and practice
are based on notational analysis, which typically identiﬁes
the who, what, where, and when of key game events.2
