Review article 
 
Unlocking the power of set pieces in men’s professional football – a 
scoping review

ABSTRACT 
 
Set pieces represent a crucial moment in football analysis but have yet to receive as much 
attention as other football moments or physical and physiological elements. This 
systematic review summarized the literature surrounding set-pieces in professional 
football players. The studies were included if the sample comprised adult male football 
players competing in tiers 3 to 5, and set pieces were examined (i.e., penalties, corners, 
free kicks, throw-ins).

A total of 95 studies met the eligibility criteria. Most studies 
investigated penalties (44%) and corners (20%), whilst free-kicks and throw-ins have not 
yet to be examined extensively. Characteristics of penalty kicker, penalty placement, 
goalkeepers’ actions and contextual factors affected the accuracy of penalties. Corners' 
success was dependent on the type of delivery (i.e., inswing or outswing) the number of 
players in the penalty area and contextual factors.

Constraints associated with the task, 
individual and environment were associated with the execution of free kicks. Throw-ins 
seemed essential to keep the ball in possession, although the literature was scarce. The 
characteristics of set pieces should take into account the defensive organization of the 
opposing team, as they are particularly important for creating goal-scoring opportunities 
and influencing the match result.

Keywords: performance, penalties, corners, free-kicks, throw-ins, ecological dynamic 
model

INTRODUCTION 
Performance analysis, particularly in football, gained popularity in the last 
decades in order to understand the interaction of tactical, technical, physical, and 
psychosocial dimensions at four levels of analysis [1-3]. Advancements in technology 
(video tracking and microsystems) and the growth of platforms to record data (i.e., Stats 
Performance, Stats Boom) were associated with increased scientific publications 
surrounding performance analysis in football.

An early review identified 53 papers about 
match analysis in football [4]. Studies focused on describing physical, technical, and 
tactical actions, comparing players of contrasting competitive levels or by playing 
positions, or creating predictive models to explain performance in football [4]. An update 
of this review in 2018 organized the studies following the ecological dynamics framework 
[5].

This demonstrated substantial differences in variables of interest and technology used 
to examine activity profiles, set pieces and interactions between players [5, 6]. 
The literature in football has focused on describing the physical and physiological 
demands [7-10], characterizing external load by playing position [11-14], examining the 
influence contextual factors on physical demands [15-17], and describing team 
behaviours [18, 19].

Of the three dimensions proposed by Sarmento et al. [6], set pieces 
have received less attention in the context of football analysis. During a football match, 
when the ball goes out of play or play is interrupted due to fouls, the game is restarted 
through set pieces. There are a range of set pieces in football, including penalty kicks, 
free kicks, corners and throw-ins, which can often represent match defining moments 
[20].  
The importance of set pieces during a football match is recognized by coaches and 
clubs [21, 22] and documented in goal statistics of national leagues [23-25] and 
international competitions [26, 27].

The analysis of 32 matches during the 2004 European 
Championships showed that 36% of goals were preceded by set pieces [27]. While during 
the 2018 FIFA World Cup, set pieces accounted for around 50% of goals scored [28]. In 
the English Premier League, corner kicks and indirect free kicks were used as the second 
and third methods to score goals [23], and throw-ins were associated with ball-possession 
retention and chances of scoring a goal after successful first contact with the ball [29].

The comparison of physical and technical parameters of winning and losing teams in the 
2014 FIFA World Cup indicated that set-pieces were decisive in scoring a goal, whilst the 
influence of physical parameters was negligible [26]. Set pieces represented 8% and 3.5%

of the points attained by bottom and top elite teams, respectively [24]. Set pieces appear 
to often represent critical moments of the match and can be the determining factor in 
deciding match outcome [30]. Therefore, the current review aimed to: (1) understand the 
impact of set-pieces in football; (2) describe characteristics of successful of set-pieces; 
(3) identify literature gaps as well provide practical applications for coaches.

METHODS 
This scoping review was developed according to Cochrane guidelines [31], 
PRISMA 2020 guidelines [32] and the PRISMA-ScR extension for Scoping Reviews 
[33]. The protocol was developed by three authors (HS/FC/DVM) and registered on the 
Open Science Framework (doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/9TN3V). 
 
Eligibility criteria 
 
 
We only included original peer-reviewed articles, and no restrictions were 
imposed concerning publication date.

Eligibility criteria followed the Participants, 
Intervention/Exposure, Comparators, Outcomes and Study Design (PICOS/PECOS) 
framework: (1) Participants – male football players classified as tier 3 to tier 5 according 
to the Participation Classification Framework [34]; (2) Intervention/Exposure – 
description, intervention or exposure in relation to set pieces in football (i.e., penalty 
kicks, free kicks, corners and throw-ins); (3) Comparator – not applicable; (4) Outcomes  
– performance outcomes related with the execution of set–pieces, participants 
characteristics or environmental conditions; (5) Study – no restrictions were defined on 
the types of study designs eligible for inclusion.

Information sources and search strategy 
 
Four electronic databases were searched on November 2023, including, PubMed, 
Scopus, SPORTDiscus and Web of Science (all databases). The search strategy was as 
follows: 
 
[Title]: football OR soccer

AND 
[Full text]: “corner kick” OR “Free Kick” OR “penalt*” OR “set-piece*” OR “set 
play*” OR “throw-in*”  
 
 
Study selection 
 
 
Study selection was done using a reference management software (EndNoteTM). 
Duplicates were automatically removed and manually checked to ensure the omission of 
duplicates with precision. Two authors (HS/JB) independently screened the title, abstract, 
and reference list of each study to locate potentially relevant studies.

A third external 
reviewer (DVM) was consulted to resolve any discrepancies regarding the selection 
process. The full text of the included studies was then screened by two authors (HS/JB). 
Where disagreements occurred, a third author was consulted for arbitration (DVM). 
 
Data items and data extraction 
 
Two investigators (HS/JB) organized and conducted the data extraction and 
collected the relevant information using a predefined template.

A third researcher (DVM) 
cross-validated the data and summarized the extraction. For each study, the following 
information was recorded: citation details, study purpose, participation classification 
framework [34], country, primary results, funding, and conflicts of interest. The results 
were organized into the following five categories 1) penalties, 2) corner, 3) free-kicks, 4) 
throw-ins, and 5) studies that combined multiple set-pieces.

Data synthesis 
 
After organizing the studies by the type of set piece analyzed, a narrative summary 
of each paper was created. The information was presented in tables detailing the 
characteristics of each study and compiled in figures combining the competitions 
involved in the analysis along with the tiers of soccer players.

RESULTS 
 
Study identification and selection 
 
The initial searches identified 1,172 papers, of which 679 records were duplicates. 
As a result, 1,093 studies were screened (title and abstract). Subsequently, 970 did not 
meet the inclusion criteria and were excluded. Finally, 123 papers advanced to full-text 
analysis, of which 28 were not included in the present review for the following reasons: 
(1) did not contain set piece data (n = 12); samples included participants classified in tier 
1 or tier 2 (n = 9); (3) data were based on female players (n = 7).

In total, 95 papers were 
included in the current review (Figure 1). 
 
[Figure 1 – about here] 
 
Study characteristics 
 
Studies were grouped according to the investigated set pieces: penalties, corners, 
free kicks, throw-ins and studies analyzing multiple set pieces. Figures 2 and 3 show the 
main characteristics of studies included in the current review. Penalties and corners were 
investigated in 44% and 20% of the studies, respectively.

Some studies focused on free-
kicks (7%) and throw-ins (2%). Penalties (71% of studies) and corners (37% of studies) 
were mainly investigated across multiple competitions. Multiple competitions included 
studies that examined the same competition on different occasions (e.g. World Cup 2002, 
World Cup 2006, World Cup 2010) or different leagues (e.g. Premier League, Bundesliga, 
La Liga, Ligue A).

A minority of studies focused on analyzing set pieces in a specific 
competition. Most football players were classified as tier 5 (World Class) or tier 4 
(Elite/International). For studies analyzing penalties, nine of them used players competing 
at the national level (tier 3). 
 
[Figure 2 – about here] 
[Figure 3 – about here]

Results of individual studies 
 
 
Penalties 
 
 
Studies analysing penalties [35-76] were organized into three topics: 1) penalty 
kicker characteristics or behaviors, 2) goalkeeper actions, and 3) contextual factors (Table 
1).  
 
Penalty kicker 
 
 
Seven studies focused on the technical parameters of the players [40, 41, 43, 47, 
53, 59]. Body position and penalty preparation (i.e. running speed, length of run) were 
common characteristics investigated among penalty takers [40, 41, 43, 47, 59].

Slow 
running speed was described as a feature of penalty kickers of the big five leagues 
(English Premier League, German Bundesliga, Spanish La Liga, Italian Serie A, French 
Ligue 1) and Champions League players [41]. In La Liga, most of the penalties were shot 
after the adoption of a static position and were preceded by three steps [43]. A significant 
percentage of players in two studies tend to take penalties with the right foot [43, 59]. 
Right-footed players place many penalties to the right side of the goalkeeper, and left-
footed players tend to place the ball to the goalkeeper's left [49, 59].

Variation across 
studies concerning zone placement and where the penalty has more chance of being 
successful was noted [36, 43, 44, 59]. 
Three recent studies showed that success in penalties was higher when the penalty 
was placed in the lower zones, and the probability of missing a penalty increased when 
the penalty was placed in higher zones of the goal [36, 43, 44]. However, considering 
players of contrasting competitive levels, penalties taken by elite players to higher zones 
of goal have more chance of success [59], and goalkeepers recognized them as being more 
difficult to stop [67].

The two crucial factors for penalty success were time [60, 61] and 
gaze behaviour [51, 68]. Spending a greater duration of time adjusting the ball, reacting 
to referee signals, and avoiding behaviour (i.e., not observing the goalkeeper directly) 
were also associated with better performance. Studying goalkeeper tendencies prior to the 
match [63] and higher skills [35] increased the probability of penalty scoring.

Pressure 
and anxiety were frequently reported during the penalty event [55, 70, 72].

Goalkeeper actions 
 
Five studies confirmed that the influence of anticipation of the shot is a 
determinant to increase the chances of saving the penalty [39, 54, 58, 74, 75].  Information 
received by the goalkeepers [39, 58] and experience in penalties [39] were defining 
aspects for anticipating the penalty placement. Another characteristic of successful 
goalkeepers is the ability to maintain the position for as long as possible before the penalty 
[61, 67, 74, 75].

One study verified that distracting a penalty taker increased the 
probability of missing a penalty by 10% [51]. 
 
Contextual factors 
 
Different contextual factors were investigated surrounding penalty taking (i.e. 
type of competition, match result, time, pressure, training, previous performance, 
popularity of players) [46, 37, 45, 47, 48, 51, 52, 56, 65, 66, 73, 76]. Pressure decreases 
performance, and the presence of fans in stadiums influences penalty conversion [35, 38, 
76].

Studies also found that players with a higher public status performed worse on 
penalties [64, 65]. 
 
[Table 1 – about here] 
 
Corners 
 
 
The studies of corners are organized into two groups: successful corners and 
contextual factors [77-95]. The frequency of corners per match is low. However, this set 
piece is decisive for the match result and team performance [79, 83, 84, 87, 89].  
 
 
Successful corners 
 
 
Successful corners were dependent on the type of delivery (inswing or outswing) 
[77, 79, 91], the zone where the corner was covered [79, 91], the number of players within 
the penalty area [79, 81, 87], and the absence of defensive interventions [80].

Contextual factors 
 
 
The positioning and number of offensive players in the box during corner kicks 
depend on various contextual factors (i.e. match result and minutes to finish the game) 
[85, 91] (Table 2). Another decisive factor explaining the great number of corners and 
attempts at goal from corners was match location [88].  
 
[Table 2 – about here] 
 
Free kicks  
 
 
Seven studies [96-102] investigated direct or indirect free kicks (Table 3).

Four 
studies tested the effects of physical environment [96], mental fatigue [97], spatial 
variables [99], and practice [101]. The three remaining studies focused on understanding 
which variables are determinants of free kicks [98, 100, 102]. Physical environment, 
mental fatigue, type of play, players in the wall, distance to the wall, and rule violation 
changed the characteristics of free kicks [96, 97, 99].

Indirect free kicks substantially 
impact match results, with the offensive organization being critical to the success of this 
set piece [98, 100]. 
 
[Table 3 – about here] 
 
Throw-ins 
 
Only two studies focused on throw-ins [29, 103]. Both studies confirmed that 
throw-ins were mainly used to maintain ball possession (Table 4). Pressure applied during 
the throw-in allowed the defending team to recover the ball [103].

Longer throw-ins 
tended to be less successful [29]. 
 
[Table 4 – about here]

Multiple set-pieces 
 
 
This section includes studies exploring multiple set pieces [104-128] (Table 5). A 
considerable number of studies showed the increase and importance of set pieces in 
football [108, 112, 113, 115, 117-119, 123-126, 128]. The relevance of a specific set-
piece varied across leagues and competitions. The time to perform the set-pieces was 
influenced by the quality of the team [109], match result [109, 127], and zone of the field 
wherein the set-piece was awarded [127].

[Table 5 – about here] 
 
DISCUSSION 
 
This systematic scoping review provides a synthesis of the literature surrounding 
set pieces in football. Set-pieces were widely recognized as decisive during a football 
match outcome, although, the importance of each set-piece varied across the competitions 
analyzed. The final outcome of a penalty success is dependent on the penalty taker, 
goalkeeper and contextual factors.

Type of delivery (i.e., inswing or outswing) and 
tactical decisions (i.e. number of players within the penalty box) are determinants of 
successful corners. Free kicks are influenced by factors associated with the type of play, 
players in the wall, distance to the wall, offensive organization, players’ mental fatigue 
and environment. The characteristics of throw-ins are integral to maintaining ball 
possession and creating chances at goal.

Data surrounding free-kicks and throw-ins are 
limited. Therefore, these set pieces need particular attention in further studies. These 
insights can be useful for coaching in implementing a data-led approach to set-pieces to 
optimize the likelihood of success in matches. Professional clubs are increasingly 
recruiting specialized coaches for set pieces, which highlights the importance of this 
review.

Set pieces appear to represent a significant proportion of goals scored across the 
big-five leagues in Europe [105, 110-112]. The impact of each set-piece varied across 
studies depending on the competitions analyzed. For example, the combination of 1409 
goals derived from 576 matches in the 2020/2021 Premier League and La Liga season 
concluded that corners were linked with 36% of the goals scored [79] though there was a 
higher percentage of corners overall in the English Premier League [105].
The

comparison of goal patterns scored between the 2009/2010 and 2018/2019 seasons in the 
English Premier League, La League, Serie A, Bundesliga, and Ligue 1 showed large 
differences between leagues [112]. Whilst throw-ins were decisive in Spain and corners 
in England, indirect free kicks represented a significant percentage of goals scored in 
Germany and penalties in Italy [112]. Therefore, studies on set-pieces should report their 
relevance considering the competition analyzed.

Often for the studies including multiple 
set-pieces (Table 5), the data were combined across different seasons, rather than 
presented separately [108, 117, 123, 128]. Determining the evolution of set pieces and 
the changing patterns across seasons could present integral insights into the changing 
trends in football. A retrospective analysis of attacking actions in elite football confirmed 
the growing importance of set pieces from 1966 to 2018 [108].

Time spent on taking 
throw-ins and free kicks also increased from 2004 to 2016 [123] and were often used as 
a tactic to cause interruptions in the match, typically for time-wasting purposes [127]. 
These two studies demonstrated the necessity of practicing set pieces regularly during 
training sessions and confirmed the significance that coaches place on throw-ins and free 
kicks. Additionally, when a team is losing and attempting to regain ball possession, it is 
advisable to avoid throw-ins and free kicks.

Penalties and corners were the most explored set-pieces in football. Although 
studies investigated different aspects related to these set pieces in isolation (e.g. body 
position, preparation, type of delivery, players within the penalty area), the combination 
of different studies following the ecological dynamic framework in sport [129] should be 
used to organize the performance analysis in football [6].

The basis for explaining sports 
performance is the functionality between the individual and the environment, which 
permits the coupling of perception and action during set pieces. The success of penalties 
is not only dependent on the penalty taker (finishing foot, a zone where the penalty is 
placed) but also on the perceptions retrieved from the environment (i.e. pressure, anxiety, 
fans in the stadium) and interaction with goalkeepers [130].

Maintaining the position for 
as long as possible [39, 54, 58, 74, 75] and anticipating the penalty attempt [62, 71, 74, 
75] were identified as two main characteristics of successful goalkeepers which both 
require an interaction with the penalty shooter.  
 
The type of delivery was an aspect that was explored for corners. Two studies 
using data from Portugal [79] and US leagues [91] noted that in swinging corners were

the most frequent type of deliver, while one study from the Greek Super League found 
that out swinging corners increased the chances for successful attempts on [77]. An 
increase in the number of players within the box appears to be related to the success of 
corners [77, 79, 91], even though the presence or absence of defenders, as well as match 
time or result also determined the result of the corner [80, 85, 91]. The interaction between 
these variables necessitates further investigation: (1) Is the type of delivery on corners 
(i.e., in-swing or out-swing) influenced by the number of players in the box, defensive 
organization, or the individual characteristics of the players?

(2) What factors determine 
the choice of foot for corner-taking? Free kicks were a determining set piece concerning 
match outcome in national and international competitions, including, the Premier League 
[110], Bundesliga [112], MLS [116], La Liga [117], and FIFA World Cup [114].  Mikael 
Arteta, the Arsenal coach, highlighted the significance of free kicks particularly when 
facing teams that defend with low blocks: “A lot of teams are defending with low blocks, 
so open play is one thing, but set pieces aren’t something very different to the game.

It’s 
something that is connected, so it’s as important, because against low blocks we are going 
to generate more free kicks and more corners.” [131]. From the studies extracted in the 
current review, it is evident that individual fatigue, wall distance, number of players in 
the wall, temperature and altitude are decisive in explaining the performance of free kicks. 
Coaches and performance analysts should spend time investigating the constraints 
associated with offensive and defensive corners and free-kicks and design exercises that 
represent the task characteristics within the performance environment [129, 130].

The present study provides a broad overview of the literature focused on set 
pieces. Most of the studies investigated a considerable number of competitions, using 
different teams and covering the big five leagues in Europe as well as the most important 
international competitions (i.e., the European Championships and FIFA World Cup). 
However, the present review included players from tier 3 to 5, which could be considered 
a limitation as the current perspective might not apply to players competing in the lower 
leagues of football.

This notion also applies to females, as the present work focused solely 
on males. We also largely overlooked the types of studies that focused on the subjective 
interpretations, including, coach and player views on set pieces, which might be key to 
accruing a deeper understanding on the ‘why’ involved with decisions made around set 
pieces. However, doing so allowed us to focus on objective outcomes concerning what 
results in set-piece success.

The current review highlights the importance of set pieces in football and suggests 
that coaches and performance analysts should include the practice and analysis of set-
pieces during training sessions and match preparation [6, 132]. Context should be 
addressed in relation to the relevance of the data, since a number of studies drew different 
conclusions depending on the individual league and/or competition analyzed.

Coaches 
can use the set piece summaries in the review to inform players which aspects need to be 
prioritized during training sessions. Following the ecological dynamic framework, studies 
of set pieces corroborate the impact of different constraints (individual, task and 
environment) on the success of set pieces. These constraints must be included in training 
sessions to create a representative learning practice.

CONCLUSION 
 
Set pieces are an important tactical element to consider in weekly planning, as 
they represent significant and effective goal-scoring opportunities that can determine the 
outcome of a match. This scoping review indicates that set pieces should be strategically 
planned to destabilize the opponent's defensive organization and exploit vulnerable areas 
within it. Understanding how in-swing and out-swing corners may lead to distinct 
outcomes is crucial for coaching and performance analysis. Right-footed and left-footed 
players may demonstrate different proficiencies in delivering in-swing or out-swing 
corners, depending on the side of the field.

Therefore, teams' capacity to defend various 
corner types can vary, making this information valuable for match strategy—particularly 
in deciding which corner types to use and who should take the corners. Constraints 
associated with set pieces influence effective playing time and should, therefore, be 
considered in both individual and team strategic behavior, such as whether to pursue or 
avoid set pieces based on the match result.

Furthermore, this knowledge should be 
cultivated during player development to enhance their understanding and execution of set 
pieces.
